How Capitalism Produces Political Backlash

Stephen Weymouth

Dean’s Professor

2026-11-09

On September 15, 2008, Lehman Brothers filed the largest bankruptcy in U.S. history. Within weeks governments were rescuing the banks.

Timing: 0–3 minutes.

  • Lehman listed $639 billion in assets and $613 billion in debts (History.com). U.S. unemployment rose from 5.0 percent in December 2007 to 10.0 percent in October 2009 (BLS).
  • On November 4 the class saw how economic decline in particular places became political. Today opens with a puzzle (the next two slides) and Wolf’s answer: the financial crisis and the rescue that followed.
  • Photograph: reporters outside Lehman Brothers’ headquarters in Midtown Manhattan on the night of September 15, 2008.

[Sources] - Martin Wolf, The Crisis of Democratic Capitalism (2023), ch. 4, pp. 99–110. History.com, “Lehman Brothers collapses” (updated May 28, 2025); BLS, “The Recession of 2007–2009,” February 2012. Background photograph: Robert Scoble, Lehman Brothers headquarters, September 15, 2008, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0, resized.

Capitalism’s popularity has fallen in the U.S.

Gallup, Socialism’s Positive Rating Tops 40% for First Time, September 2026.

Small business still has a 95 percent positive rating, while big business has fallen to 35 percent.

Why would people in the world’s largest market economy think less of capitalism?

Timing: 3–6 minutes. Pose the key-line as the session’s puzzle and do not answer it yet; Wolf’s chapter is the answer.

  • Chart, percent positive (Gallup): capitalism 61 (2010), 61 (2012), 60 (2016), 56 (2018), 60 (2019), 60 (2021), 54 (2025, the series low), 55 (2026); socialism 36, 39, 35, 37, 39, 38, 39, 43 (2026, the series high and the first reading above 40).
  • Same survey, 2010 to 2026: big business 49 to 35, free enterprise 86 to 77, small business 95 to 95.
  • Survey: August 3–24, 2026, 1,200 adults by telephone, margin of error plus or minus 4 points. Gallup first asked in 2010, two years after the crisis, so there is no pre-crisis reading.

[Sources] - Gallup, Lydia Saad, September 23, 2026; Gallup, September 8, 2025; series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json; original drawing.

Young adults now rate socialism above capitalism

Among adults under 30, capitalism’s positive rating fell from 68 percent in 2010 to 45 percent in 2018.

From 2010 to 2026 Democrats’ rating of capitalism fell from 51 to 35 percent, while Republicans’ rose.

Today’s young adults grew up during the crisis or the slow recovery that followed it.

Gallup, Socialism’s Positive Rating Tops 40% for First Time, September 2026.

Timing: 6–9 minutes. Ask what “socialism” means to someone who was ten years old in 2008; take two answers, then move on.

  • Chart, 2026, percent positive, capitalism and socialism: ages 18–34, 43 and 57; 35–54, 50 and 45; 55 and older, 65 and 34. Gallup changed its age groups, so the 2026 groups do not match 2010’s.
  • Ages 18–29: capitalism 68 (2010) and 45 (2018); socialism 51 in both years (Gallup, August 13, 2018).
  • By party, capitalism positive (party identifiers without leaners): Republicans 71 (2010) and 75 (2026); independents 61 and 56; Democrats 51 and 35. Democrats’ socialism rating: 50 and 65. The 2026 rise in socialism’s rating came entirely from independents (Gallup).
  • Keep the discussion on what the words mean to respondents and why views moved; do not ask students their own views or party.
  • The key-line’s link to the crisis is the instructor’s reading; Wolf does not discuss young adults or socialism. In 2010 adults under 30 rated capitalism at 68, above the national 61, so the decline came during the slow recovery rather than right after the crisis (Gallup, 2018).

[Sources] - Gallup, September 23, 2026; Gallup, Frank Newport, August 13, 2018; series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json; original drawing.

Your IB Voice

The crisis and capitalism

Positive views of capitalism in the U.S. have slipped since 2010, most among the young. Using one piece of evidence from Wolf, explain how the 2008 financial crisis could have changed the way people judge capitalism.

10 minutes · Individual · Notes permitted

Timing: 9–19 minutes. Leave the prompt up for the full ten minutes.

  • Passages students will reach for: households with flat or falling incomes (p. 102); the rescue of “both banks and bankers” while families lost homes (p. 104); the crisis made failures visible and “clearly the fault of certain specific elite institutions and people” (p. 109).

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), pp. 102, 104, 109.

What did the crisis cost households?

Timing: 19–19 minutes.

Output per person never returned to its old path

World Bank, World Development Indicators, 2026: GDP per capita, constant 2015 dollars; trend fitted to 1990–2007.

After 2009 the U.S. economy grew again, but never fast enough to return to its old path.

The U.K. fell furthest behind; Wolf judges its loss larger and longer lasting than either world war or the Great Depression caused.

The crisis lowered the path that living standards were expected to follow, not just output for a year or two.

Timing: 19–22 minutes. Ask what an American household would notice about a $12,600 gap per person. Then ask which is worse: a deep recession that recovers to the old path, or a shallow one that never does.

  • Chart: U.S. real GDP per person, constant 2015 dollars (World Bank). Actual: $39,200 (1990), $54,150 (2007), $51,860 (2009), $61,050 (2019), $67,950 (2025). Trend fitted to 1990–2007 grows 2.2 percent a year and reaches $80,560 in 2025, so the 2025 gap is about $12,600 a person, 16 percent (instructor’s calculation).
  • Other countries, percent below their own 1990–2007 trend in 2025 (same method): United Kingdom 35, Spain 30, Canada 27, Italy 23, France 19, United States 16, Germany 8, Japan 2. Germany and Japan grew slowly before the crisis, so they had less to lose relative to trend.
  • Wolf’s figures for 2018 (Conference Board data): Spain 24, U.K. and Italy 22, U.S. and Canada 17, France 13, Japan 7 percent below trend; Germany had no significant shortfall (pp. 100–101). Wolf’s Japan trend is 1.8 percent a year (Conference Board, p. 100), twice the World Bank-based trend.
  • Wolf: the U.K.’s shortfall is “a substantially bigger and more permanent loss” than either world war or the Great Depression caused (p. 101).
  • Part of the gap after 2020 reflects COVID; most of it opened between 2008 and 2019 (U.S. 14 percent below trend in 2019).

[Sources] - World Bank, WDI, NY.GDP.PCAP.KD, retrieved November 5, 2026; series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json; original drawing. Wolf (2023), pp. 100–101, Figure 21.

Most households’ market incomes stopped rising

On average across 25 rich countries, about two-thirds of households earned no more from work and savings, after inflation, in 2014 than in 2005.

These are incomes before taxes and government transfers.

Economic stagnation is a long period in which output and most people’s real incomes barely grow.

Wolf, The Crisis of Democratic Capitalism, 2023, Figure 22, p. 102, from McKinsey Global Institute.

Timing: 22–25 minutes.

  • Figure 22, percent of households with flat or falling real market incomes, 2005–14: Italy 97, U.S. 81, U.K. 70, Netherlands 70, France 63, Sweden 20, average of 25 advanced countries 65 (Wolf: “between 65 and 70 percent,” p. 102). The figure is Wolf’s own, cropped from the book.
  • After taxes and government transfers, incomes were flat or falling for 20 to 25 percent of households on average, and for under 2 percent in the U.S. and Sweden, where governments offset the fall in market incomes (McKinsey Global Institute, 2016, executive summary).
  • Unemployment: U.S. 4.6 percent (2007) to 9.6 (2010); eurozone 7.6 (2007) to 12.1 (2013); Italy 12.8 (2014), still 10 in 2019; Spain 26.1 (2013), still 14.1 in 2019 (pp. 102–103).
  • Wolf on expectations: rising prosperity “from generation to generation” was the purpose these societies claimed for themselves (p. 86, earlier in the chapter).

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), pp. 86, 102–103, Figure 22 (reproduced from p. 102), citing McKinsey Global Institute (2016).

Governments cut deficits during a weak recovery

Redrawn from Wolf, The Crisis of Democratic Capitalism, 2023, Figure 24, p. 104 (IMF data); values read from the figure.

Each arrow runs from a government’s largest structural deficit between 2007 and 2017, which for most countries came in 2009–11, to its smallest deficit afterward, mostly in 2013–17.

A structural deficit is the deficit a government would run if the economy were at full capacity.

Austerity is cutting spending or raising taxes to shrink a budget deficit.

Timing: 25–28 minutes.

  • Chart: Wolf’s Figure 24 redrawn as arrows from each country’s largest structural deficit to its smallest, 2007–17, percent of potential GDP, approximate (bar heights measured on the figure). Tightening (the length of each arrow): Greece 17.2, Spain 8.8, Portugal 8.1, U.K. 6.9, U.S. 6.1, Japan 4.8, Canada 4.8, France 3.8, Italy 3.8, Germany 3.5. Largest and smallest deficits: U.S. −9.2 and −3.1, U.K. −8.7 and −1.8, Greece −12.1 and +5.1, Spain −10.6 and −1.8. Wolf’s figure does not give the years of each peak and trough; for most countries the largest deficit came in 2009–10, while unemployment was still high.
  • Wolf: the recession and weak recovery raised spending and cut revenue “relative to precrisis expectations”; the G7 “all imposed significant structural fiscal tightening,” largest in the U.S. and U.K.; “only countries savaged by the eurozone crisis, especially Greece, experienced greater structural fiscal tightening” (p. 103).
  • A structural balance (the measure in the figure) strips out the effect of the business cycle, so tightening reflects policy choices rather than recession.

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), pp. 103–104, Figure 24, citing IMF; redrawn in color from values read off the figure, series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json.

Why did the crisis cost so much trust?

Timing: 32–32 minutes.

Banks were rescued while families lost homes

Paulson and Bernanke, Congressional Testimony, 2008

In October 2008 Congress authorized $700 billion to rescue financial firms.

By 2013 about 4.8 million homes had been lost to foreclosure, yet only one Wall Street executive went to prison (Credit Suisse’s global head of structured credit).

A corporate bailout uses public money or guarantees to keep a failing firm alive.

Timing: 32–35 minutes.

  • Wolf: the public saw “the resources of the state used to rescue both banks and bankers,” while they suffered foreclosure, unemployment, stagnant wages, and austerity; “essentially nobody (or nobody of any importance) was punished” (p. 104).
  • TARP: $700 billion authorized October 3, 2008 (Emergency Economic Stabilization Act); cut to $475 billion by Dodd-Frank in 2010; about $444 billion disbursed (CRS; CBO).
  • Foreclosures: about 4.8 million completed from September 2008 to the end of 2013, against roughly 250,000 a year before the crisis (CoreLogic, January 2014).
  • Prison: Kareem Serageldin, Credit Suisse’s global head of structured credit, was sentenced on November 22, 2013 to 30 months. From August 2007 to February 2008 his group marked a book of subprime mortgage bonds above market prices to hide more than $100 million in losses (the plea release says as much as half a billion), which helped secure his bonuses; Credit Suisse then wrote down $2.65 billion. He pleaded guilty to conspiring to falsify the bank’s books and records, forfeited $1 million, and paid a $150,000 fine (U.S. Attorney, SDNY, April 12 and November 22, 2013). He was convicted of hiding losses, not of causing the crisis. ProPublica called him “the only Wall Street executive sent to jail for his part in the financial crisis” (April 30, 2014).
  • Photograph: Henry Paulson (left) and Alphonso Jackson before a House hearing on the mortgage crisis, September 20, 2007, a year before the rescue.

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), p. 104. CRS R41427 (June 27, 2013); CBO, “Final Report on the Troubled Asset Relief Program” (April 19, 2024); CoreLogic (January 29, 2014); ProPublica (April 30, 2014); U.S. Attorney’s Office, Southern District of New York, press releases 13-128 (April 12, 2013) and 13-365 (November 22, 2013). Photograph: David Valdez, U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, September 20, 2007, via DPLA and Wikimedia Commons, public domain, resized.

Confidence in banks collapsed after 2008

Gallup, Confidence in Institutions, 2026: banks.

Confidence in banks halved between 2007 and 2009 and has not returned to its precrisis level.

Wolf argues that a visible failure, followed by a rescue of those blamed for it, caused the distrust.

Timing: 35–38 minutes.

  • Chart, percent with a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in banks: 60 (1979), 36 (1990), 53 (2004), 41 (2007), 32 (2008), 22 (2009), 21 (2012, the record low), 38 (2020), 28 (2026).
  • Wolf: “Most policy mistakes in economics are invisible to the bulk of the voting public,” but this one could not be missed; many came to believe the failures reflected “intellectual and moral corruption” among decision-makers (p. 104).

[Sources] - Gallup, Confidence in Institutions, retrieved November 5, 2026; series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json; original drawing. Wolf (2023), p. 104.

Home prices fell by more than a quarter

S&P Dow Jones Indices, S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index, via FRED, 2026.

For most homeowners the house was their largest asset, so the fall erased much of their wealth.

Owners who owed more than their homes were worth could not sell or refinance, and millions lost them to foreclosure.

The housing crash turned a banking crisis into a loss that ordinary families felt directly.

Timing: 3 minutes.

  • Chart: S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index, not seasonally adjusted, January 2000 = 100. Peak 184.6 (July 2006); low 134.0 (February 2012), a fall of 27 percent. Adjusted for consumer prices (CPI-U), the fall was 35 percent. The index passed its 2006 peak again in 2016–17.
  • Prices nearly doubled from 2000 to 2006 (100 to 185), so families who bought near the peak lost the most.
  • Foreclosures: about 4.8 million completed from September 2008 to the end of 2013 (CoreLogic, January 2014), the figure on the bank-rescue slide.

[Sources] - S&P Dow Jones Indices LLC, S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index (CSUSHPINSA); U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI-U (CPIAUCSL); both retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, November 9, 2026; series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json; original drawing. CoreLogic, January 29, 2014.

The rescue that made money

The Treasury got back more from the banks it rescued than it put in, while TARP grants to help homeowners avoid foreclosure cost $31 billion. Why did the bank rescue still cost so much trust?

Timing: 38–42 minutes.

Answer key:

  • CBO (April 2024): TARP’s total net cost was $31 billion; financial institutions including AIG returned a net gain of $9 billion; credit-market programs a net gain of $3 billion; autos cost $12 billion; mortgage and housing programs cost $31 billion. Treasury’s bank support programs disbursed $245 billion and returned $276 billion.
  • Wolf’s reasons: the public saw bankers, the “architects” of the disaster, rescued while they lost homes and jobs, and saw no one important punished (p. 104).
  • The rescue protected creditors, shareholders who were not wiped out, and executives’ jobs; homeowners received a smaller and slower program. Fairness, not the budget, decided the verdict (instructor’s interpretation).

[Sources] - CBO, “Final Report on the Troubled Asset Relief Program,” April 19, 2024; Treasury Office of Financial Stability, FY2023 budget document; Wolf (2023), p. 104.

Trust in the federal government has stayed low

Pew Research Center, Public Trust in Government: 1958–2025, 2025; 2008 is the average of three polls.

Trust in the federal government fell long before 2008, and the crisis kept it near its lowest levels.

Democratic capitalism pairs a market economy with elected government, and each depends on citizens’ trust.

How can the crisis of democratic capitalism be overcome?

Timing: 42–45 minutes.

  • Chart, polls compiled by Pew: 73 (1958), 77 (1964), 36 (1974), 25 (1980), 44 (1984), 60 (October 2001, after September 11; 31 in January 2001), 31 (2007), about 25 (2008: the average of three autumn polls, 17 CBS/New York Times, 31 National Election Studies, 26 CNN), 22 (2010), 19 (2015), 17 (2019), 16 (2023), 22 (2024), 17 (September 2025). Pew’s own moving average for 2008 is 24 to 25.
  • Wolf’s chapter opens: trust in democratic institutions, the global market economy, and elites “has faded over recent decades,” shown in protectionism, hostility toward immigration, and “authoritarian populism” (p. 83).
  • The definition on the key-line is the instructor’s summary of the book’s argument.

[Sources] - Pew Research Center, December 4, 2025; series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json; original drawing. Wolf (2023), p. 83.

In 2011 “Occupy Wall Street” protesters camped near Wall Street and said they spoke for the 99 percent.

Timing: 45–46 minutes.

  • Occupy Wall Street began in Zuccotti Park on September 17, 2011.
  • Wolf, earlier in the chapter: from 1993 to 2015 the top 1 percent captured 52 percent of the increase in U.S. real pretax incomes (p. 91).
  • Photograph: a speaker at Occupy Wall Street, New York, 2011.

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), p. 91. Background photograph: David Shankbone, Free Speakout, Occupy Wall Street, 2011, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0, resized.

Why did the backlash come after 2008?

Timing: 46–46 minutes.

Populist parties in Europe gained after the crisis

Redrawn from Wolf, The Crisis of Democratic Capitalism, 2023, Figure 25, p. 108 (data from Roberto Foa); values read from the figure.

In southern Europe, where the euro crisis hit hardest, populist support was flat for a decade and rose most after that crisis began.

Populism casts politics as a contest between a virtuous people and a corrupt elite.

Timing: 46–49 minutes. Ask what changed in 2008 that had not changed in 1998; take one answer before the next two slides.

  • Chart, approximate (traced from Wolf’s Figure 25), population-weighted percent: southern Europe about 14 (1995), 15 (2007), 23 (2008), 28 (2013), 38 (2015), 45 (2018); northern Europe about 6 (1995), 8 (2007), 10 (2010), 15 (2015), 21 (2018).
  • Wolf introduces the figure with his question about cultural change: “Why should all this have become so salient now?” His answer: “something big happened: the financial crisis and its aftermath” (p. 108).
  • The southern jump between 2007 and 2008 matches Italy’s April 2008 election, five months before Lehman failed, so do not present that step as a response to the crisis; the later rises (2012–18) follow the euro crisis (instructor’s reading of the figure).
  • Definition: Cas Mudde’s widely used minimal definition, populism as an ideology that separates society into “the pure people” versus “the corrupt elite.”

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), p. 108, Figure 25, citing Roberto Foa; redrawn in color from values traced off the figure, series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json. Cas Mudde, “The Populist Zeitgeist,” Government and Opposition 39, no. 4 (2004): 541–563.

The foreign-born share grew less in the U.S.

Political scientists Inglehart and Norris call populism a cultural backlash against social change.

Wolf replies that these changes ran for decades, so culture alone cannot explain why the backlash came when it did.

Wolf argues that immigration became far more political in the U.S. only after the crisis.

World Bank, World Development Indicators, 2026: international migrant stock, from UN DESA.

Timing: 49–52 minutes.

  • Chart, foreign-born share of the population, 2000 and 2015, with change in points: New Zealand 17.8 to 24.5 (+6.7); U.K. 8.0 to 13.9 (+5.9); Australia 22.9 to 28.1 (+5.2); Canada 17.9 to 22.4 (+4.5); Germany 12.7 to 15.4 (+2.7); U.S. 12.4 to 14.7 (+2.3).
  • Wolf: the increase in the foreign-born share was “strikingly low in the US after 2000” and the share “modest” compared with Australia, Canada, and New Zealand (p. 109). Immigration from the new Commonwealth began in the 1950s; Enoch Powell’s speech was April 20, 1968 (p. 109).
  • Pippa Norris (2016, quoted on p. 113): populist authoritarianism is “a cultural backlash in Western societies against long-term, ongoing social change.” Inglehart and Norris (2016): “It would be a mistake to attribute the rise of populism directly to economic inequality alone” (p. 107). Kaufmann goes further: right-wing populism “has little to do with economics” (p. 107).
  • Wolf’s reply: “The crucial difficulty with primarily cultural explanations is that they fail to provide an answer to the obvious question: Why now?” (p. 107). On p. 110 he adds that the crises “crystallized the anger and distrust that had been building up in previous decades over (often interlinked) economic and cultural changes.”

[Sources] - World Bank, WDI, SM.POP.TOTL.ZS, retrieved November 5, 2026; series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json; original drawing. Wolf (2023), pp. 107–110.

Financial crises

Funke, Schularick, and Trebesch, “Going to Extremes: Politics after Financial Crises, 1870–2014,” European Economic Review, 2016.

In the five years after a financial crisis, far-right parties’ vote share grows by about a third: a party that won 10 percent before the crisis wins about 13 percent after it. Ordinary recessions do not produce this jump.

Why would a banking crisis matter more?

What do your friends mean by socialism?

Timing: 56–56 minutes. Return to the age chart from the opening (young adults rate socialism above capitalism).

Your friends and socialism

  1. Think of a friend or acquaintance who says socialism would work better than capitalism.
  2. Describe what that person most wants changed. Share with a partner.
  3. Discuss whether the complaint fits Wolf’s explanation - or if something else is the main factor.
  4. Decide what 1) a company and 2) a government could do to earn that person’s trust.

15 minutes · Individual then pairs · Reading permitted

Timing: 56–66 minutes. Pairs. Students talk about a friend, not themselves, and do not name the friend. Do not ask students for their own views or party; if a student volunteers a view, treat it like any other claim.

Answer key:

  • What young adults mean: asked in December 2025 to name something good about socialism, 13 percent of adults aged 18 to 34 said “nothing,” against 42 percent of those 55 and older; 29 percent of 18–34s named equality, against about 20 percent of older groups, and about a quarter named basic services such as health care, education, and housing (Gallup, Saad, August 6, 2026). In 2018 the most common meaning of socialism was “equality” (23 percent); “government ownership or control” was 17 percent, half its 1949 share of 34 percent (Gallup, Newport, October 4, 2018).
  • What they dislike about capitalism (all adults, December 2025): greed 24 percent, benefits the wealthy or too much inequality 23 percent, corporate power 21 percent (Gallup, August 6, 2026).
  • Wolf’s explanations: today’s young adults grew up during the crisis and the slow recovery (stagnation, pp. 101–103); the rescue protected “both banks and bankers” while families lost homes (p. 104); distrust of those in charge (pp. 104, 109).
  • Expect complaints the reading does not cover (housing costs, student debt); these are the “neither” answers, so note them as outside Wolf.
  • A company earning trust (instructor’s examples): pay that rises with productivity, competing on price and quality rather than market power, and no rescue at public expense.

[Sources] - Gallup, Lydia Saad, “How Americans View Capitalism, Socialism and Free Enterprise,” August 6, 2026 (Gallup Panel web survey, December 1–14, 2025, about 666 adults per system); Gallup, Frank Newport, “The Meaning of ‘Socialism’ to Americans Today,” October 4, 2018; Wolf (2023), pp. 101–104, 109.

Discussion

In 2026, 69 percent of adults aged 18 to 34 viewed “free enterprise” positively, but only 43 percent viewed capitalism positively. What does that gap tell us about what some young people don’t like?

Timing: 66–78 minutes. Whole class. Take three or four pairs’ one-sentence complaints, then put the question to the room. Write two columns on the board: complaints about markets and complaints about who gained and who paid.

  • Gallup, August 3–24, 2026: ages 18–34, free enterprise 69 percent positive, capitalism 43, socialism 57; all adults, free enterprise 77, capitalism 55, big business 35, small business 95.
  • What separates the two words is inequality: in December 2025, 23 percent named “benefits the wealthy” as something bad about capitalism, against 9 percent for free enterprise, while greed (24 and 22) and corporate power (21 and 24) were named about equally. Each respondent was asked about only one system (Gallup, August 6, 2026).
  • Expected answers: many friends reject big business, inequality, and rescues for the wealthy rather than markets or private property; that is close to Wolf’s account of distrust after 2008 (p. 104). Some will want public provision of health care or housing, which is a different claim and worth separating.
  • Push back if the room settles too quickly: socialism’s rise in 2026 came from independents, and Gallup has no reading from before 2008 (notes on the opening slides).

[Sources] - Gallup, Saad, September 23, 2026 and August 6, 2026; Wolf (2023), p. 104.

Module 7 takeaways

How does globalization produce political backlash?

Offshoring raises national income through wage arbitrage, but the losses fall on particular workers.

Those losses spill over into the local economies where the workers live, and those places turned to populists.

After 2008 economic stagnation left most households’ earnings flat for years.

A corporate bailout rescued the banks while families lost homes and jobs, which turned disappointment into distrust of elites.

This distrust weakens democratic capitalism; young adults now rate socialism above capitalism.

Timing: 84–90 minutes. Before each click, ask the room for its answer, then reveal the line. All four lines are today’s; November 2 and 4 (offshoring, local spillovers) are not repeated. Lines one, two, and four use today’s syllabus key concepts: economic stagnation, corporate bailout, and democratic capitalism. Line three returns to the opening puzzle: Wolf explains why trust fell after 2008; the Gallup data show that among the young and Democrats the response was to think less of capitalism, while Wolf’s chapter follows the voters who turned to right-wing populists (pp. 114–115, outside the assigned pages, explains why the right gained more). End in open discussion on the last line.

  • Wednesday, November 11, opens Module 8, how shocks travel through global business: Peter S. Goodman, How the World Ran Out of Everything, chs. 3, 10, and 18.

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), pp. 99–110; Gallup, September 23, 2026.
